content: If medications for generalized onset seizures are not available, monotherapy with either phenytoin or phenobarbital may be considered. For focal onset seizures, lamotrigine or levetiracetam should be offered as first-line treatment for both children and adults with epilepsy. If neither lamotrigine nor levetiracetam is available, carbamazepine should be used as an alternative first-line treatment for focal onset seizures in these populations. If the initial monotherapy is unsuccessful, an alternative first-line monotherapy should be tried. Lacosamide can be offered as a second-line monotherapy for focal onset seizures if none of the first-line medications are effective. If antiseizure medication monotherapy fails in individuals with generalized or focal onset seizures, prompt referral to a specialist is recommended to explore other treatment options. For generalized onset seizures, high-certainty evidence suggests no statistically significant difference in time-to-seizure remission among various antiseizure medications (ASMs), including carbamazepine, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, phenobarbital, phenytoin, sodium valproate, and topiramate. Given the risks associated with sodium valproate in women and girls of childbearing potential, lamotrigine or levetiracetam should be used as first-line treatment in this population. Carbamazepine has similar efficacy to other ASMs, including levetiracetam and lamotrigine, but lamotrigine and levetiracetam are now preferred for focal epilepsy due to their better side-effect profiles and comparable efficacy. The choice of ASM depends on seizure semiology, and outcomes are reported separately for focal onset seizures (with or without awareness, or focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures) and generalized onset tonic-clonic seizures (with or without other generalized seizure types such as myoclonus or absence seizures). All ASMs considered (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, topiramate, gabapentin, sodium valproate, levetiracetam, lacosamide, zonisamide, phenytoin, phenobarbital) are effective in controlling seizures. Broad-spectrum ASMs, such as lamotrigine, topiramate, sodium valproate, levetiracetam, lacosamide, zonisamide, and phenytoin, are effective against multiple seizure types. Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are primarily used for focal onset seizures but can be effective against generalized tonic-clonic seizures in individuals with generalized onset epilepsy, although they may exacerbate other seizure types in these individuals. Gabapentin is not appropriate for generalized epilepsy and should only be considered for focal onset seizures. No systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing these ASMs with placebo was found, as it is considered unethical to conduct RCTs comparing standard ASMs with placebo in established epilepsy due to the need to treat epilepsy to reduce morbidity and premature mortality. Both levetiracetam and sodium valproate are effective against all seizure types and may be ASMs of choice when the type of seizure or epilepsy syndrome is unclear. All ASMs are associated with adverse effects, with phenobarbital linked to a higher risk of shortand long-term tolerability issues. Sodium valproate, when taken during pregnancy, is associated with a significantly higher risk of fetal malformations and hepatic side effects, such as elevated transaminases and ammonia levels. Sodium valproate is contraindicated in individuals with liver disease. Phenytoin, despite being used as a first-line drug in some settings, has a problematic pharmacokinetic profile and is associated with risks of arrhythmia and hypotension, making it challenging to administer in adults with comorbid cardiac conditions. Most trials excluded pregnant women, as seizures during pregnancy may be due to eclampsia, requiring different treatment strategies. Women and girls with epilepsy who are of childbearing potential should be offered lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for both generalized and focal onset seizures. Valproic acid (sodium valproate) is not recommended in this population due to potential harm to the fetus. Women with epilepsy should have their seizures controlled as effectively as possible with the minimum dose of ASMs taken in monotherapy whenever possible. Standard breastfeeding recommendations remain appropriate for women with epilepsy taking the ASMs included in this review (phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproic acid, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, topiramate, lacosamide). Most ASMs are associated with higher risks of major congenital malformations in offspring of women taking these medications during pregnancy compared to controls not taking ASMs. Sodium valproate, phenobarbital, phenytoin, and carbamazepine are associated with higher risks of major and minor congenital malformations. Topiramate is linked to higher risks of major congenital malformations, but no information is available on minor congenital malformations. There is no data on the teratogenic effects of lacosamide. High-quality studies on side effects related to ASM exposure exclusively through breast milk are lacking, but the amount of ASM in breast milk is extremely low, and the baby is likely to have been exposed to the same ASM(s) in higher concentrations in utero. Women and girls of childbearing potential prescribed sodium valproate should be advised to use effective contraception without interruption for the entire duration of treatment. They must be provided with information on pregnancy prevention and the risks associated with sodium valproate use during pregnancy and referred for contraceptive advice if they are not using effective contraception. If a woman taking sodium valproate is planning to become pregnant, a specialist trained in managing epilepsy in pregnant women should consider alternative treatment options. Every effort should be made to switch from sodium valproate to an appropriate alternative treatment before conception. If switching is not possible, the woman should receive further counseling regarding the risks of sodium valproate for the unborn child to support her informed decision-making. Nocturnal supervision should be considered for the prevention of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). SUDEP is defined as sudden, unexpected, witnessed or unwitnessed, non-traumatic, or non-drowning death of people with epilepsy, with or without evidence of a seizure, excluding documented status epilepticus, and in whom postmortem examination does not reveal a structural or toxicological cause for death. This intervention is particularly appropriate for individuals with convulsive seizures arising from sleep. Nocturnal supervision involves the presence of an individual of normal intelligence and at least 10 years old in the bedroom or the use of special precautions such as regular checks throughout the night or a listening device. This intervention is low-cost and associated with limited anticipated risks. People with epilepsy should be encouraged to adhere to their ASMs, avoid sleep deprivation, limit alcohol consumption, and refrain from recreational substance use to reduce the risk of seizures and seizure-associated mortality. They should also exercise caution to minimize the chance of injury during a seizure, such as avoiding baths and opting for showers or strip-washes instead. Those with sleep-related seizures should avoid sleeping in a prone position to reduce risks associated with sleep seizures.
